versation between a farmer and a student of finance-the student, I suppose, being the Canadian Bankers' Association. Then further on there is a reference to the western farmers being misled by uninformed agitators. Well, I think this legislature was misled by a lot of uninformed agitators when members were told that a bank could not fail without the depositors being protected. Otherwise I do not believe this parliament would ever have passed the act giving them their charter. All the cards should have been laid on the table. Parliament gave to the Canadian Bankers' Association tremendously wide powers. - Let me mention a few of the purposes of the association as set out in the act of incorporation:
(1) to promote the interests and efficiency of banks and bank officers, etc.; (2) to establish sub-sections of the Association; and (3) to establish clearing-houses for banks, by-laws regarding which require the consent of the Treasury Board. More serious powers were those imposed by the Bank Act. When the banks undertook to guarantee the note issue of every bank they found that they needed the power to inspect the note issue records of each bank and some protection at the moment of the suspension of a bank. For these purposes the Bank Act gives the Association power (1) to appoint a curator to supervise the affairs of any bank which may suspend payment, until the resumption of its business or the appointment of a liquidator; (2) to supervise the issue of bank-notes, including the making, delivery and destruction of the notes, and the inspection of the circulation accounts of the banks; (3) the custody and management of the Central Gold Reserves; and (4) to impose penalties for the breach or non-observance of any by-law, rule or regulation made by virtue of the section of the Act in question.
So that to all intents and purposes the Canadian Bankers' Association to-day have the powers of parliament, and instead of having only a Senate and a House of Commons in this country we have a Senate, a House of Commons and a house known as the Bankers' Association. Among the vast powers given to them under the act is that of inspection. But they did not inspect; they led us to believe everything was safe. Now, they say that the depositors of the Home Bank have no claim, but in my opinion they have a good moral claim. This legislature is responsible for the position in which these poor people who have lost everything now find themselves. They put their money in the bank because they thought they were protected. Let me quote just here the words of the Right Reverend Bishop Fallon of London in this connection:	.
But how can this end be reached in the matter under consideration. By the simple method of making the banks collectively responsible for the money they accept as deposits. The banks borrow our money without other security than the charters the people give them; they pay no, or a very low, rate of interest. When they loan us our money they charge
us the highest rate of interest obtainable, and every shred of security that can be squeezed from us is rigorously exacted. We are actually made financial slaves by the very power of our own savings. And the bankers gamble with our earnings, and tell us to go whistle when the crash comes.
No	further faith	can be put in	those	who havebeen	hitherto our	financial guides.	They	have beenweighed and found wanting. And they know it themselves. We are now being told that the banks have	no objection	to " government	inspection," butthat	the government must bear	the	consequent
" responsibility." The people of Canada will not tolerate the placing of any such " responsibility " on their government, that is, on themselves. They shall demand an effective guarantee for their hard-earned savings, and they will look to the forthcoming session of the federal parliament to exact that effective guarantee from those to whom these savings are confided.
I had a resolution on the order paper, Mr. Speaker, asking the government to consider the advisability of assisting the depositors and of calling upon the Canadian Bankers' Association to that end, but the motion has been ruled out of order on the ground that it involves a matter of finance. In my opinion, if the Canadian Bankers' Association will not voluntarily come across with this money, their association should be assessed for the amount of loss sustained through their failure to carry out proper inspection and audits and to maintain a state of efficiency in the banking business. Hon. members of this House should put their heads together and see what can be done to bring about some active measure of relief for these unfortunate depositors, many of whom lost their all and can never get back to the position in which they were before. I hope that this parliament will take such steps as may be necessary to restore confidence in the banking system of the country, and will see to it that the Canadian Bankers' Association carry out the conditions under which they received their charter. I suggest that should they fail so to carry out those conditions, parliament should take their charter from them and vest those powers where in my opinion they should be vested, in the Finance department of this country.
Mr. FRANK S. CAHILL (Pontiac):	I
agree with much that has been said by hon. members on both sides of the House with regard to the desire on the part of every person that the Home Bank depositors should be reimbursed if it is at all possible. I am not one of those who believe that our banking system is the last word in banking; I think that some useful amendments could, be made to the Bank Act, amendments that would serve a good purpose in this country. Only a very few years ago we had twice as many banks
Home Bank Investigation

in Canada as we have to-day. We had then a much better banking system than we have at the present time. The smaller banks in Canada are gradually being absorbed by the larger until it is perfectly obvious that within a very few years we shall have not more than three or four very large banks in Canada, serving the people by a system of branch banks. I do not believe that that system will serve the people in developing this Dominion. The branch banks to-day are merely gathering points for deposits. These deposits in turn are sent on to head office for investment. It is quite apparent to any person who will study the Canadian banking system that it would be impossible for these branch banks to make loans in the country; the system will not permit it. Some of our banks have three or four, and some as many as seven hundred, branches throughout Canada. They select a boy from school in the country, put him in the bank as messenger, later on he becomes an accountant, and in a very few years he blossoms out as a branch bank manager, with absolutely no experience in any kind of business except book-keeping and the making up of interest. Under the present system of banking a branch bank manager can make a good showing for his branch by not lending one cent from his branch. He can do that in this way: If he can get sufficient deposits in his bank to forward to head office he will be allowed enough interest on that to show a profit in his branch, and he does not need to lend a cent out of his branch. The result is that the cautious boy adopts that course and sends the deposits to head office. The money that is deposited in the branch banks all over Canada is forwarded to head office, and head office makes the loan.
I did not agree with much that was said in the Banking and Commerce committee last year about the banks not wanting to make loans. It goes without saying that no bank can make a profit and succeed unless it does make loans, for the only way they make a profit is by making loans, and the only way in which you can obtain a loan under the present system is by going to head office, where the money is accumulated from the branches. As a result of this accumulation, head offices have from time to time made improvident loans, and the bank failures in Canada in the past have been caused by head office loans. The money accumulates at head office, and if they cannot make legitimate loans they do what was done recently in the case of-the Home Bank, make speculative loans where the ordinary business man would say they have no chance of recovering their capital. The Home Bank failure has 
brought to the notice of the Canadian people more forcibly than anything else the shortcomings of our banking system, but the Home Bank failure did not disrupt the business of this country to anything like the extent it was disrupted by the Merchants Bank fiasco. When the Merchants Bank closed its doors there were hundreds of thousands of customers and depositors who had to look elsewhere for their banking connection. They had to make new banking arrangements^ start all over again in the tedious business of building up a credit.
Let me say that I have no grievance against the bankers of this country. I have never in my life made an application to a bank for a loan that was refused. I could always get all the money I wanted from the bank, so I have no grievance on that score.

Can the hon. gentleman
tell me how he did it?

I shall be glad to, because
it will illustrate one of the points I want to bring out. After I had made a few loans at first, as my business developed and I required more money I did what everyone else does who wants to get a loan; I went to head office. You cannot get money any other way. The branches have no authority to make loans under the present system, and unless a man who wants to borrow money can get acquainted with the officials at head office his business is in a very precarious state, because he cannot get anywhere with the branches.

How is it that no money
would bd' advanced to my hon. friend where he is best known and that he could get all the money he wanted where he was not known?

knows as well as I do that every man has to be recommended by his home office before he can get to head office, so there is nothing in my hon. friend's contention. Apparently he is not able to get recommended at either place.
We are told that we have the best banking system in the world, that we have very few failures. I have been told repeatedly that in the United States this past year there were four or five hundred failures of banks. That would mean forty or fifty bank failures in Canada, in proportion to our population, and as a matter of fact we have had sixty or seventy bank failures in Canada in the past year. The failure of each branch of the

Home Bank is the failure of a bank just as much as the failure of an individual bank at any point in the United States. They have several systems in the United States, and I am not competent to speak with authority on any of them, but I do know that in some of the states where the branch bank system is operating-not on the same lines as ours but along similar lines-they have had more failures than in other states where branch banks are not permitted.
I believe that the motion of the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) is very good, but I think that instead of referring this matter to a special committee his motion, or something similar, should be referred to the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce, and I therefore propose to move an amendment:
That all the words after the word " That " be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
In the opinion of this House, in view of the failure of the Home Bank and of the fact that official prosecutions and inquiries have been instituted, including the royal commission which has been appointed to investigate the facts alleged in the petition represented by the shareholders of the bank and the affairs of the bank generally, and considering that the evidence received and to be taken before the several tribunals will be available for consideration, the Select Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce should be instructed to consider the provisions of the Bank Act, with a view to recommending such amendments to the act as will better protect the interests of the depositors generally and will prevent similar occurrences in the future; and also to consider the report of the royal commission in its bearing upon these matters and with respect to the possibility of saving the Home Bank depositors from loss.
I think that will serve the purpose better than my hon. friend's resolution.

I propose to support a motion which will enable the standing committee on Banking and Commerce to consider this question, not in the autumn-even if a special session is called for it, which we know will not take place-not next year or the year after, but this session. The amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Cahill) simply means that the hands of parliament are to be entirely tied for an indefinite period. We may just as well cut out the camouflage and get down to facts. My hon. friend talks about the evidence to be got from trials and the like, the help that will be given to the committee. He asks the committee to wait until this royal commission has royally functioned, and he ties the hands of parliament just as absolutely and effectively as if the motion itself, was defeated. What is the need of the commission at all? What is the need of putting the question at all if the matter is
to be so determined? Why, the whole thing has been inquired into, threshed over backwards and forwards. And what is to prevent the banking committee at any time taking up any question on banking? The thing is a farce and is intended as a farce-that and nothing else. Wait until the trials? Why there is to be a case tided before the Privy Council some time this summer, in the early summer, to find out how these fellows are to be tried; then after all that you have to get your trials. Let us be honest about this thing. Let us start in by trying to be a little honest about it. We can have no action now-action of any and every kind would be impossible now-if that amendment is accepted. That is the way, Mr. Speaker, which this amendment strikes me. It rather carries on the whole game the government is playing in connection with this bank.

It is idle to say that there are no liars; but because we find a liar here-

It would be absolutely wrong to say that they were all liars over there. Some of them may be honest and I think they are. fallacy of it. In one part of his speech he tells us that the banks are in this deplorable condition. In the next part of his speech he takes the position that the banks are so well off and prosperous that, without affecting their depositors or the interests of their shareholders, they can afford to shoulder the whole burden. My hon. friend is wrong there. He is right in this-that it is always better to have open and free discussion. The bank that ought to be respected has nothing to hide. Therefore, the position that I take is, in short, this, that any investigation into the Home Bank ought to be full and thorough; it ought to have to do, not only with its governmental connection during a certain period of its lifetime, but most particularly with its birth, and then, a great deal more emphatically and particularly, with its death. Further, if anything is to be done in connection with this matter, it is a great deal better that it should be done now. Why leave in the public mind the suspicion that people are giving voice to, that members of this House are giving voice to, as to the solvency of our institutions?

In the opinion of the hon. gentleman, would it be possible for the Banking committee or any other select committee during this session of Parliament to investigate fully the affairs of the Home Bank and to come to a definite conclusion as to its condition at the time it was formed, as to the maner in which it conducted its business and as to the shape in which it was when it went into liquidation?
They can do that at least as quickly as any royal commission, and there is no reason why they should not get to work, stick to it, and do it.
They cannot finish it.

I do not know why they could not or should not. In any event, they will have to do it sooner or later. Whatever work is done by any royal commission, if anything is wrong, has all to be done over again before that committee. No measure of relief or change in the law can be carried out by the commission. Any fences that are found to be down cannot be re-erected by the commission. In any event, the work has to be done by the committee. If the government wants to have the commission running around, all right; but if we are really serious about this, we should say one of two things: Either that because there is a royal commission, nothing is to be done until that commission reports in so many words-and that means that we shall do nothing this year-or we should reject the amendment

Home Bank Investigation moved by the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill). '

speakeroldname: Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think
the admission of my hon. friend the former Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) is one of the most peculiar utterances ,t we have ever heard in this House on a serious question. Altogether it is rather a unique situation that an hon. gentleman speaking for the opposition should have been a Minister of Finance of this country during a period in which he ought to have known something about this bank. It is generally understood that my hon. friend had in his possession certain information that had been given to Sir Thomas White in previous years, and I think many in this House would view with some suspicion this attempt to sidetrack a deliberate effort which I believe the House will appreciate on the part of this government to find out the true facts in regard to the whole situation and to take action immediately those facts are found. That is the policy of this government. Imagine my hon. friend intimating to this House that the sole purpose of the organization of the commission was to get after Sir Thomas White. That is a peculiar statement, and one which my hon. friend knew, when he made it, had no warrant in fact.
My hon. friend says I made a statement which I knew to be untrue when I made it?
No.

What did he
say.
No warrant in fact. That is what I said.

He said that I
knew it had no warrant in fact. I now ask for a ruling from the Chair whether that is a parliamentary expression.

I think the Minister of
National Defence said that what had been stated by the hon. gentleman was not warranted in fact. I did not catch the words "that he knew."
"To my knowledge."

The Minister of National Defence said, and very emphatically, that the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry
Drayton) had made a statement which, at the time he made it, he knew had no warrant in fact. That is a distinct violation of the rules, even though supported by the laughter of hon. gentlemen behind.
Do I understand that my hon. friend says that he did not know that there was no warrant in fact for his statement?
I have asked for a ruling.

No hon. gentleman can
impute motives, and if the Minister of National Defence said that the hon. gentleman knew that the statement was not warrant in fact, that is not parliamentary.

I will say
this, that if my hon. friend did not know it, he ought to have known it, because if my hon. friend had taken the slightest trouble-
I would ask the Chair to request the hon. member to withdraw his statement.
I will ask the hon. gentleman if he will withdraw that statement.

Certainly. And I will show this House before I finish the few remarks I have to make that my hon. friend ought to have known there was no warrant for that statement. He knew there was presented to the government a petition from-

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. The rule is of no avail whatever if that is to be considered a withdrawal. I ask again for a ruling as to whether anything the minister has said is a withdrawal in any sense whatever.
He has withdrawn the statement. He made a sign.
I did not hear it.
Yes, he withdrew the statement.
Certainly.
If the minister says he has withdrawn, I am satisfied.

Certainly. My hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) knew that there had been a petition presented to the government on behalf of sixty thousand depositors who had lost their money in the Home Bank. That petition was

Home Bank Investigation
presented by a representative delegation of men from all parts of the country, from British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec. It was in the following terms:
To His Excellency General the Right Honourable Lord Byng of Vimy, G.C.B., G.C.M.G., M.V.O., Governor General of the Dominion of Canada, in Council.
The petition of the undersigned members of the Executive Committee of the depositors in the Home Bank of Canada, humbly sheweth:-	.
(1)	Your Petitioners are residents of various parts of the Dominion of Canada and are the duly appointed executive committee representing about sixty thousand depositors in the Home Bank of Canada.
(2)	The said Bank was a Chartered Bank doing business under the provision of the Bank Act. Your petitioners are informed and believe that in the years 1915 and again in 1916 and in 1918 representations were made to the Department of Finance of the Dominion of Canada respecting the condition of the Home Bank of Canada and revealing a state of affairs that would have justified an investigation by the Department of Finance under the powers conferred upon the Minister of Finance under Section 56A of the Bank Act, whereby he was authorized to examine and enquire specially into any of the affairs or business of the Bank.
(3)	Your Petitioners realize the seriousness of such action on the part of the Minister of Finance, and that the mere fact of causing an audit to be made might in itself bring about the failure of the said bank.
(4)	Your Petitioners are also aware that at the time such representations and disclosures were made, the Country was at War and that the Minister of Finance, having regard to the public interest, was unwilling to precipitate a bank failure or crisis, or in any way disturb the financial condition of the Country, and that for such reason and on other good and sufficient public grounds, may not have deemed it advisable to exercise the power above referred to.
(5)	If such audit had been made your Petitioners believe that the condition of the Bank would have been shewn to be such that its continuance in business could not have been further permitted.
(6)	Your Petitioners believe that if the said Bank had ceased doing business at the time the said disclosures were made the then existing assets would have been almost, if not quite sufficient to meet all claims of creditors, whereas, by reason of the Bank continuing in business until the 17th day of August, 1923, and greatly increasing the amount of money belonging to the public on deposit, and at the same time permitting the assets of the said Bank to be greatly diminished in proportion to the amount of the deposits, the present depositors have suffered and will unless relief is granted, suffer a very severe loss.
(7)	Your petitioners submit that the reasons an audit was not made of the said Bank, in accordance with the powers vested in the Minister of Finance, were reasons of a public and national character, and intended for the benefit of the public at large, and that therefore the loss to the present depositors occasioned by the Bank being permitted to continue to do business should be borne by the public at large and not by the present depositors.
(8)	The said Bank and its predecessors. The Toronto Savings Bank and the Home Savings and Loan Company had for over fifty years been regarded as a safe depository for the savings of the public and the class of people who deposited their money in the said Bank was largely composed of wage earners with small earnings and their deposits consisted in many cases of the whole savings of a life-time.
(9)	Your Petitioners submit that the confidence of the simple people throughout Canada in the banking

institutions of the country is of the very greatest importance to the industrial and commercial interests of the country and that the lack of such confidence would have a serious and detrimental effect on the whole industrial and commercial prosperity of the country.
(10)	Your Petitioners therefore submit that whether rightly or wrongly the depositors of the Home Bank of Canada were largely of the opinion that the Finance Department of the Govermnent of Canada exercised such supervision over chartered Banks that it was impossible for depositors to lose their savings entrusted to such a bank the charter of which had been renewed from time to time by parliament and it is further submitted that the confidence of the people as a whole would be greatly restored if adequate relief were granted to these depositors.
Wherefore your petitioners pray that your Excellency be pleased to submit to Parliament an Act for the full indemnity of the depositors of the Home Bank of Canada against any loss suffered by reason of the failure of the said bank.
And your petitioners as in duty bound will ever pray. Dated this 23rd day of January, 1924.
W. T. J. Lee.
Edgar C. Sanders,
R.	M. G. Anglin, E. H. Cleary,
W. A. Dover,
J. A. Sinclair, Henry Winfield, Arthur English,
S.	S. Henderson,
H. H. Higginbotham, A. B. Campbell,
Paul Poisson,
A. G. Browning, W. T. Kernahan. J. H. Mitchell. J. C. Brudy,
J. O. Reilly,
J. F. Edgar,
J. P. Greacy,
W. A. Buchner, J. I. Weedon.
The delegation which presented that petition, made up, as I have said, of representative men from all parts of the country, alleged that in the years mentioned in the petition the attention of the then Minister of Finance, Sir Thomas White, had been called to the condition of the bank, and they asserted that instead of performing his duty under the provisions of section 56a of the then Bank Act, he made no audit such as was contemplated, and that had he taken this course a situation would have been disclosed which although it would probably have caused the failure of the bank, would have enabled the depositors to be reimbursed. That was their case. Therefore they claimed that on principles of justice and fair play they should be paid their deposits. They presented for the consideration of the government an interview which was given by Sir Thomas White to the Canadian Press, in which he admitted that he had received representations in regard to the bank, but gave the war and other reasons-I need not quote the interview in detail; most of it is unquestionably known to hon. gentlemen-as his justification for not having an audit made.
Now, I leave it to the judgment of every hon. member as to what was the duty of this government under the circumstances. Would the government have been justified, without any investigation, in asking parliament to vote the money necessary to compensate the

Home Dank Investigation
depositors for their losses? If, without a full and complete investigation, they had done so, then they would have been making (he Treasury liable not merely to those who lost money in the Home Bank, but to those who had lost money in the Farmers' Bank and in all other bank failures which had occurred in the history of the Dominion. Well, what was to be done? Was not the most natural and ordinary thing to do to make an investigation into the truth of the allegations set out in the petition? It was when we decided to make that investigation, in making which my hon. friend says, we were taking a political course entirely in order to get after Sir Thomas White.
Hear, hear.

In the face
of the petition presented to us, does my hon. friend mean to say there was any other course open to the government than the course we adopted of ordering a judicial investigation?
Certainly.

Mr. Speaker, what was the course adopted by the government of Sir Robert Borden in 1912, when allegations were made by the depositors of the Farmers' Bank which had recently failed with regard to the circumstances under which its charter was granted? Sir Thomas White himself was the finance minister at the time, and he and his friends cannot now complain if we have followed what he then recommended-Sir Thomas White recommended to Council the appointment of the late Sir William Meredith, then Chief Justice of Ontario, to examine into the truth of the statements contained in the petition. We have taken the same course to-day.
Then when parliament meets my hon. friends opposite say:	"Oh, you are not investigating this thing completely enough." Well, we started out to do what the depositors wanted us to do. We took the position that if the statements contained in their petition were proved to be correct by the Chief Justice of New Brunswick, a jurist of high repute, then the government would be bound to take some action in regard to the matter. But my hon. friends come along and say:	"We don't want to find out what
these depositors want to find out; we want everything investigated from the beginning to the end."

If the government was so anxious to do just what the depositors asked, may I ask whether this sentence was put in at the request of the depositors:
-without in an way accepting the view that in the circumstances mentioned it is proper for the government to expend public moneys in the relief of the depositors of the said bank.

I have no doubt that the same clause was inserted in the order in council appointing Sir William Meredith. We were not going to prejudge the case; by that statement we simply reserved to ourselves the right to act upon this matter when the commissioner reported. If we were to decide in advance that we were going to pay the money without any investigation, then-
You are having an investigation.

My hon.
friend knows that very well. We simply reserve our judgment until we have an investigation made by Chief Justice McKeown into the allegations made by the depositors. If we find that those allegations are true, then the government will have to consider what course to pursue. We appointed a commission; the commissioner has made full arrangements; he has given up his circuit in New Brunswick and begins his hearings in Ottawa on April 16. He is prepared also to go to Toronto in order that full evidence may be heard. Was there anything wrong in our course up to that point? Did a single depositor find fault with us for taking that course? What other course could we have taken? If the commissioner had had nothing else to do than inquire into the statements made in the petition, there is no reason why we could not have had a report from him within a very short time. But my hon. friends come along and they want all sorts of things inquired into, which may not have the slightest relevance to the question whether or not the country should contribute any money to the depositors. The depositors have made their case; they have submitted their argument, and we are finding out the facts. We are prepared to act either on an interim report or upon the final report when presented, which we hope will be at the earliest possible day.
The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) to a certain extent is involved in this matter. As a result of the representations made by hon. gentlemen opposite, the powers of the commissioner have been extended-
-to an investigation of the affairs of the said bank during the whole interval between the issue of the bank's charter and the failure of the said bank, including any representations made to the government of the day, as to its condition, any action taken by any of the ministers of finance upon such representations as may have been made, and the effect on the position of the depositors of any audit under Section

Home Bank Investigation

56a of the Bank Act if made at any time in consequence of such representations.
So my hon. friend's conduct as Minister of Finance comes under review before the commission.
Not in the first order, but in the one we wanted.

My hon.
friend did not know what he wanted.
Yes, he did.

He did not know anything about the order until we brought it here. He talked about having wide investigations. We are willing to have wide investigations-anxious to have them. But we do not want the case of the depositors as presented to us-and because it involved Sir Thomas White we are told we are playing polities in investigating the matter-to be imperilled or interfered with; we do not want anything to prevent its full consideration by the commissioner and his early report thereon to the government.
Now, my hon. friend, speaking of the amendment of the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill), said that it meant that nothing could be done, that parliament was tying its hands until the result of the criminal actions was known. Probably my hon. friend made that criticism simply on hearing the resolution read, and did not know just what the effect of the resolution was. In other words, he made a hasty criticism of it-and that is speaking very kindly. As I understand the resolution of the hon. member for Pontiac, it deals very fully and completely with the proposal that was brought before the House to-day by the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine).
What did the hon. member for East Calgary propose? His motion is:
That, in the opinion of this House, a parliamentary committee should be appointed immediately to investigate the Home Bank failure, with a view to discovering any weaknesses in the Bank Act which may be amended to prevent a similar occurrence: to devise some means of protecting depositors generally: and to make recommendation as to the possibility of saving the Home Bank depositors from loss.
The resolution of the hon. member for Pontiac deals with the three matters that are referred to by the hon. member for East Calgary; He recognizes the fact that investigations have been made by the curator; that investigations have been made at the request of my hon. friend, the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) that other information is obtainable from the investigation made by the Attorney General of Ontario; that the commission which we have

appointed is proceeding to function; and that the evidence taken before that commission will be available day by day to go before the Banking and Commerce committee. My hon. friend suggests that an inquiry by a commissioner will take longer than an inquiry before a parliamentary committee, But hon. gentlemen should remember that the commissioner in this case is a judge who will sit every day from ten o'clock in the morning until the usual time for the closing of the day's proceedings, and he will be attending to the one task of ascertaining the facts in connection with the allegations made by the depositors in their petition. That is his business; that is his duty. How can a committee of the House of Commons sit except in the mornings for an hour or two? How can they give full attention to this matter with hon. gentlemen giving consideration to the other important questions that come before this House? What possible attention could be given to details except by the retaining of counsel and all that kind of thing? Any gentleman who has had experience in regard to inquiries the purpose of which has been to ascertain the truth in reference to public questions will realize that a trained jurist who devotes himself exclusively to the task of getting at the truth will do so more effectively than a parliamentary committee which can only sit occasionally and do desultory work. So that as I understand the resolution of the hon. member for Pontiac, there will be committed to the Banking and Commerce committee at once the task of considering this question of the Home Bank failure, of considering the evidence adduced before the commission and of obtaining it day by day as it is given. With that evidence before them they can proceed to make such recommendations as they deem wise and which can be crystallized into legislation for the purpose of preventing a condition of affairs from arising in the future similar to that which has arisen in connection with the Home Bank, and for the purpose of protecting the rights of depositors in the future. The motion also provides that when the report of the commissioner is presented-which the government hope will be well before the conclusion of this session-the committee on Banking and Commerce will have the right to consider it and to deal with the question whether something should be done to assist the depositors in the matter of their losses. I submit that the resolution of the hon. member for Pontiac is one that ought to commend itself to the judgment of every hon. member of this House who is anxious that the interests of the public shall be protected and

Home Bank Investigation
that a full and proper inquiry shall be made into this matter. And that inquiry should first be into the facts alleged by the petitioners,-let us never get away from that; hon. gentlemen may talk about paying these losses, and it is right that they should talk about it. But when we come to consider how this matter was first initiated and brought to the attention of the government; when we remember that representatives of 60,000 depositors, who had made their organization and retained counsel, came to the government and made requests based on a certain statement of facts, I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this House will agree that this government did the wise thing in endeavouring to find out first as to the truth of the facts alleged, and the government will be prepared to act. The committee will be asked to consider the findings made by the commissioner dealing with that particular matter. It should be the first matter submitted to the commissioner.
That is the situation, Mr. gpeaker. What more could this government do? Every hon. member that sits in this House knows of hard cases that have arisen wherever the Home Bank had an agency. Pathetic stories have come to us all, of the widowed mother left alone with no money, and of organizations that have lost all their funds. Sad cases are to be found all over the country, and I am sure that every hon. member of this House approaches the consideration of this question in a most sympathetic way. I think I can speak for my colleagues as well as myself when I say that we all do so. But we want to have the matter dealt with on proper business lines. We want to have findings made by a proper tribunal, to be submitted to this House.
It is alleged that there were certain peculiar circumstances in connection with the Home Bank which were responsible for its failure. It is alleged that those circumstances were such that in the interest of the country and as a matter of fairness and justice this parliament should reimburse the depositors. It is alleged too that the circumstances in this case are different from those which existed in the case of any other bank that failed, but unless it is shown that that condition existed, in what different position are the Home Bank people from those of any other bank that has failed ever since confederation? We want to find out what the facts are, and I think we are taking the most effectual way for the purpose of getting the facts, and the government will act in this matter. The desire of the government is that the commissioner should proceed with the greatest possible speed in dealing with this question. '
It has been suggested by somebody that this government have some reason for not wanting a full investigation. As the Prime Minister has said more than once, there is not a single item in connection with this Home Bank from the period previous to the granting of its charter down to the last moment but what this government is fully prepared to have investigated. But I want to say to hon. gentlemen that those who desire to have speedy action taken in this matter do not want to have a herring drawn across the trail, as the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) attempted to do to-night in order to mix this matter up. Let the commissioner deal with this question of the request of the petitioners and report, and then let us have the fullest possible investigation of all the doings of the finance ministers during the life of the bank.
I just want to make one point more. It is alleged here that Sir Thomas White has given as a reason that he did not have the audit made which was contemplated under the old Bank Act the fact that we were at war and the danger to public credit by proceeding at that time. Now, when a duty is imposed on a minister of the Crown under a statute he is bound to carry out that duty, and if the statute does not create some exception which would enable him to evade responsibility, then he should proceed to carry out his duty. It does not make, to my mind, the slightest difference in the consideration of this question as to what reason Sir Thomas White gives why he did not act. The statute says that he could act, that the audit could be made, and he has not made the audit; that is the situation. You may excuse, you may explain, but you cannot justify. If there was given to Sir Thomas White in 1916 and in 1918 evidence from responsible and competent sources which required action on his part, it does not make a bit of difference whether the country was at war or not; I submit he should act under the statute. I only mention that because we have had discussions in this House as to whether he should or should not have acted in view of the fact that we were at war. There is nothing in the statute that exempts him or excuses him for not acting in case of war or in any other case.
Now the question before the House, Mr. Speaker, is this. Approaching the consideration of this matter, as I am sure hon. members do, or ought to do, from a sympathetic point of view, and having regard to the general interests of the whole country. I do submit that the course which the government has adopted will result in a more speedy inquiry, an inquiry which will be
Home Bank Investigation

complete and full, and which will give to the House and the country a report and information upon which we can act. The amendment of my hon. friend from Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) will * give full and complete authority to the Banking and Commerce committee to go into this whole question and enable them to report to parliament their recommendations in regard to this whole matter.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take a non-partisan stand in this debate to-night. I submit, Sir, that what is most needed to-day is the restoration of confidence in our banking institutions. To-day throughout the country business is stagnant, and men are not sure just where they are at. .1 am sorry to see this debate develop into such a partisan squabble as it has to-night.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is the func-^ tion of government to provide a sound monetary system for the country. If a government sees fit to do that by proxy, it may; but I do think that a government cannot delegate its moral obligations to banks. The government has a duty to the people which it can only discharge by providing a sound, monetary system and a thorough banking system which will be absolutely safe.
The hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) said that he was against the government reimbursing the depositors of the Home Bank because it would create a precedent, and other hon. members have taken the same view-a precedent that would be very costly to Canada. I wish to state that such a precedent would not be as costly as the repetition of bank failures has been. Some change is very, very necessary. The annual reports of our banks for the last two years have all been such as would lead the public to believe that they were all absolutely sound, and yet a number of them were in considerable difficulties. What confidence can be expected to be placed in the other banks more than in those that have been proved to be in difficulties?
Last year when the Bank Act was under discussion the banks used all their powers, which were many, in resisting the attempts of some hon. members to provide for government inspection of the banks. Now we have the evidence that some other system of inspection than prevails at present is very necessary in the interests of the banks themselves as well as of the people.
I do not think the comparison of the Farmers' Bank with the Home Bank is a fair one, as the government knew in 1916 the Home Bank was not in a sound condition.
IMr. E. M. Macdonald.)
Sir Thomas White, it is alleged, said that it was not in the public interest to permit a bank failure. I think he meant it was not in the public interest to admit a bank failure. If the Home Bank was wrong at that time, which we have every reason to believe, if it was really broke then, and that knowledge was kept from the public, I do not see why this $11,000,000 loss should be saddled on the shareholders of the Home Bank. Some say it will be eleven millions that Canada will have to shoulder and that we cannot afford it. We can afford to stand the loss of such a sum much better than the depositors can. Eleven million dollars sounds like a lot of money. It is a lot for the few depositors of the Home Bank to lose, but it is not too big an amount for all the people of Canada to pay; and if it was lost in the interest of the Dominion as a whole, if it is to be regarded practically as a war measure, then it is right that we should should*- the burden and not place that obligation on the shoulders of a few. The country is engaged in looking after the returned men and providing for them, loaning them money and financing them, because of the sacrifices they made during the war. If the sacrifices of the depositors of the Home Bank can also be regarded as a war measure, and the people of Canada benefited therefrom, I think the Dominion should come to their assistance and assume the burden.

The
constituency I represent is vitally interested in this question. At the time of the Home Bank failure we had five branches with $1,120,000 on deposit and 4,000 depositors. Now, up to the moment the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) spoke this debate had been carried on absolutely free of any political complexion of any kind. I am sorry indeed to see any hon. member of this House attempt to make the just claims of the depositors of the Home Bank a political football. No good can come from taking that attitude and I, for one, say, Mr. Speaker, that whether the charter was granted wrongfully, whether any minister of finance or officer at a later date did something, or did not do something, that he should have done is not the question that interests the depositors of the Home Bank. I have no desire to attempt to attach blame for the failure of the Home Bank to any one, or to any party; but I do say that in my opinion in seconding the amendment to the resolution I have taken the best course to protect the rights and interests of four thousand of my constituents. If it can


Home Bank Investigation
be shown, and if it is shown, that something was not done that should have been done, and for that reason this case is entirely different from some of the other failures and that it was for the benefit of the general public or for the benefit of the Bankers' Association, then I think these depositors should be paid, and paid in full.
Now, what is the best and quickest way to get relief? Are we to throw this question into the hands of a committee who can summon witnesses from all over, or is this committee to sit and duly accept the evidence that is submitted before the commissioner and duly to consider these points, and *at any time bring in a recommendation to this House? The committee may not have to wait until the final report is in before making a recommendation. If the hon. member for West York is prepared to move to-night that these depositors be paid at once without any further investigation I will support his motion. But surely no member of the House is prepared tonight to take such an attitude. If the depositors are to be paid the question comes up, who should pay them? I claim that the members of the Bankers' Association, in cooperation with the government, should pay the depositors, for the reason that if anyone was saved by the action of the then finance minister it certainly was the chartered banks of Canada. On whom would have fallen the first loss? On the chartered banks. For that reason these banks should take an entirely different attitude from what they are pursuing in this situation.
From time to time last year I attended the sittings of the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce when they were considering the Bank Act. I was not a member of the committee, but I found an atmosphere there that should not have existed. When the representatives of the people were attempting-and they do not pretend to be experts; none of us are financial experts-to amend the Bank Act I found an atmosphere of war existing, an atmosphere of war between the banks and the people of Canada-that was what existed at the sitting of the committee on Banking and Commerce. When I went there I viewed a circle of the highest-priced counsel in Canada surrounding the representatives of the people, and I felt that they were being surrounded by a bunch of high-priced gunmen. Why, some hon. members were almost afraid to open their mouths before that committee.
Not all of them.

That is not an atmosphere that should exist in this country. We are groping for light in this situation. I will admit that I would not be able to give a suggestion, because I am not an expert in banking; but I do say that from the bankers of this country a group can be got together, and a very small group, that in a very short time can show the people of this country how their savings can be ensured. The bankers of this country are the only people who can do it and do it safely. Therefore, they should co-operate with the representatives of the people, and bring the suggestion here so that we can put it in the form of legislation. That is one point.
Another point is that there should be a different method of inspection. It should not be government inspection but inspection of banks by banks. The bankers of this country can form a corps of inspectors, comprising expert government representatives whose inspection could be so thorough that it would be impossible for a single cent to be lost by the depositor, because before the capital employed in the bank would be used up from the knowledge that these men would have the bank would be closed and loss to the depositors saved. Therefore I say that with that inspection it is possible to ensure deposits. In bringing about that desirable result I am asking the co-operation not only of the bankers but of every member of this House and of every party. By carrying out this suggestion, we shall be doing what I believe the people are to-day demanding of their representatives.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext:
I desire only to add a few words at the present time to what has been said, chiefly with a view to making more clear-and placing if I can in a fail light before the House-the position of Sir Thomas White, not now a member but formerly Minister of Finance.
May I commence by saying that I have never been disposed to assume an attitude of hostility, either to the depositors on the one hand or the government on the other, in relation to this matter. I have had many delegations-well, not many but some-wait upon me up to the time of the issue of the first commission which is under review to-night, and I fancy if any of those delegates are interviewed they will say that I expressed no criticism whatever of the relationship of the government to the bank. I have had some experience in matters of this kind and I know how difficult such a situation is for an administration. I was, however, astonished
IInine Bank Investigation

when the terms of the commission were first announced. I may be wrong but I think I can divine to-night the hand that wrote the commission. I think I see behind the throne in this matter the instigator of what was intended to be a purely partisan investigation designed to injure a political opponent. Let us look over the history of the matter. The bank failed in the month of August. Many depositors over the length and breadth of our country were ruined. Others were nearly ruined. Widespread distress prevailed. People in distress are not disposed to be quite as fair-minded as they would be under other circumstances. They are disposed to grasp at anything at all that can be elevated into a complaint or a greivance, and to seek to build thereon a claim to be recouped. In doubtless this state of mind those who suffered most, the depositors, came to the government. They alleged that at a period in the prior history of the bank certain representations had been made impeaching in some way the integrity of the institution, and they alleged that had certain action then been taken the failure which they admitted would have resulted would have been less disastrous than now is the result, after some years delay. One would imagine that they had gone much further, to listen to the words of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald). One would have imagined-indeed, he stated in so many words-that they had asked for an inquiry into allegations of negligence and breach of duty, and that the government had simply acceded to their demand in granting the inquiry.

I did not
say that they had asked for an inquiry. I said they asked for the payment of the money and that the government felt that it would be necessary to ascertain the truth of the allegation before acting.

The minister went
further.
Not at all.
He stated that in asking for the inquiry they had only done what was asked for by the depositors.
Not at all.

Very well. I put myself in the judgment of the House if that was not the statement of the minister. Now as a matter of fact there was no allegation, either of malfeasance of office, of negligence or of error in judgment in any of the representations of the petitioners to this govern-
ment. Indeed, the whole body of the petition was an admission that Sir Thomas White had performed his duty in each of the decisions he had arrived at in relation to the bank. But the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) to-night has gone so far as to plainly intimate that there was a compulsion in law upon Sir Thomas White, and that to that compulsion he failed to respond and that in failing so to respond he could not plead the exigencies of the war.

What I
said on that point was this: that if a proper complaint requiring an audit under the provisions of the Bank Act, section 56 (a), as stated in the petition, was made to Sir Thomas White that he would be bound to carry out the statute; and the fact that the war was on was no excuse or justification, as it is not provided for in the statutes.

After the minister said
what I have stated, or words to the same effect, he did say what he says now; but he preceded it with the other statement. The intimation he wished to convey was that there was an allegation of malfeasance of office, an allegation of neglect of duty against Sir Thomas White, which allegation never existed and never was presented to the government,

used those words.

is a mild expression for what Sir Thomas White would have been guilty of, had the minister's words been given their full and complete interpretation. What I say is this: Lhat Sir Thomas White has not pleaded the war by way of any defence for omission of a duty he otherwise would have performed. Sir Thomas White has said that because a war was raging, because of the financial conditions that necessarily surround a ivar, he had to be all the more careful that he did not unnecessarily precipitate a financial crisis. But what I want to say to-night is this: That in order to ascertain the facts connected with Sir Thomas White's relationship to the bank, the government do not need any commission of inquiry. There were not any allegations of verbal representations and of verbal replies. What took place took place in writing and all was on the record, open to the inspection of the government, and open for their review and decision; and if upon that record they came to the conclusion that they were responsible as

That is all I have been saying right along, and if hon. gentlemen find much cause for either amusement or self-congratulation, while I admit that they are badly in need of it, I can only admire the elasticity with which they spring for it. Now may I ask the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb): Have they not now copies of all these documents in the department?

Now, Sir Thomas White in the published statement he gave, said that nothing had come to his attention which at all called for investigation under the section referred to in this debate, but that what did come to his attention came there presented by three of the directors. Those directors made certain representations to him. Pursuant to those representations, and with their full concurrence as to the method adopted, he had certain inquiries and investigations made, and the result of those inquiries and investigations was entirely satisfactory to those three directors and accepted by them as satisfactory. Sir Thomas White adds that to have made an external audit, to have sent in representatives from the outside, would in his judgment have precipitated a collapse of the bank. No lion, member would there be in this House at all acquainted with financial matters who would not agree that to take such a step is in itself very serious and likely to do very great injury to the institution under investigation. When that becomes known, to carry on further, even though the other circumstances would warrant it, would probably become impossible.
What I want to impress is this. As to what a minister of finance should do on representations made him, that minister, in association with his colleagues or alone, must decide in the light of the public interest and under the circumstances that surround him at the time. That is his duty, and his duty alone. And I want to know how any judge of the court of New Brunswick or of any other court is going to say now what a minister of finance should have done under the circumstances of five, six or seven years ago. How is he going to put himself in the position that the minister of finance v'as in then? It cannot be done. He cannot possibly surround himself with the circumstances that then prevailed, nor can he to-day revive the circumstances which surrounded the minister then. He may find out what the position of the. bank was at that time. But what were the circumstances that then surrounded the minister? The minister had to decide in the light of the representations made to him, in the light of what he knew of the record' of the Home Bank, in the light as well of the circumstances of the hour in Canada, what it was his duty to do. How is a judge of a. court now to report upon what the duty of the minister of finance was at that time? This government is in a far better position to decide than any judge. This government knows, or ought to know, something of the duties of a minister of finance. The present minister of finance knows without question, and looking over that record which reflects the

whole situation, he is in an infinitely better situation to judge what should have been done than any official of any court in Canada. Consequently I say, keeping in mind the object of the expanded order in council to ascertain whether there is liability, moral or legal, to the Home Bank depositors, the minister of finance, knowing that all is reflected in the documents, is in a far better position to determine than any judge could ever be.
But the motion of the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) goes further. As I read the order in council, while it is wide in its terms, its purpose is very definite. Its purpose was definite from the beginning, and is definite now. Its purpose, as stated in the document, is to inquire into certain things, first a few, now many, but all in order to ascertain what the government should do in relation to the depositors. I do not think any hon. member will say that there is any other object in the investigation. The object, though, of the motion of the hon. member for East Calgary is much wider. He seeks to review the circumstances of the failure for the purpose not only of seeing what ought to be done in relation to the depositors, but as well what ought to be done ip relation to the law. Consequently there is an object to be served by such investigation and inquiry that cannot be served by the present one.
Now as to the amendement. I was not in the House when the amendment was moved, but really it is an extraordinary motion, and I hope hon. members will realize its full import-what it entails if it is going to carry.
I do not think any hon. member imagines that this amendment means other than another evasion. It reads:
That in the opinion of this House, in view of the failure of the Home Bank and of the fact that official prosecutions and inquiries have been instituted, including the royal commission which has been appointed to investigate the facts alleged in the petition representing all the shareholders of the bank and the affairs of the bank generally, and considering that the evidence received and to be taken before the several tribunals will be available for consideration, the Select Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce should be instructed to consider the provisions of the Bank Act with a view to recommending such amendments to the act as will better protect the interests of the depositors generally and will prevent simlar occurrences in the future; and also to consider the report of the royal commission in its bearing upon these matters and with respect to the possiblity of saving the Home Bank depositors from loss.
Put succinctly, is it not this? That the committee on Banking and Commerce shall not hear evidence, but shall consider the report of this royal commission-when it comes; shall consider as well the evidence in the prosecutions and inquiries that have been instituted;, and upon that evidence and upon

Home Bank Investigation
the report of this commissioner shall then make recommendations to protect the interests of depositors generally and to prevent further occurrences in the future, and also with respect to the possibility of saving the Home Bank depositors.
Well, nothing apparently is going to be done by the committee on Banking and Commerce, nothing can be done until the prosecutions and appeals are over, until the other inquiries referred to, whatever they are, which have been instituted, are over too, and until, as well, this commissioner gets through the investigation of the whole history of the bank back to 1903 for his purpose of deciding what should be done about the depositors; when all these things are over they are, I presume, going to review the reports and make recommendations to this House. Well, that simply means-one can hardly tell what it means, but it certainly does mean that nothing will be done this session; it means another shelving. Hon. members talk about investigations; it means piling on top of the investigations, already so numerous, according to the Minister of Defence, still another. It will be a case of waiting until all these investigations are over and then having the Banking and Commerce committee review the matter again. Is that going to be satisfactory to the depositors? Is that going to meet the general demand of the country? Is that going to meet the demand for an answer to the question, has there been negligence; has there been malfeasance; has there been neglect of duty; has there been anything to justify or compel a recoupment of the depositors? I do not think it will, but that is the position the government takes. I protest against this continual postponement of responsibility. If the government is not able to meet its responsibility let the government get out and give place to some other which will meet responsibility. Now, the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), smiles, and sometimes as I look across the floor of the House I really think he would like to do that.

I do not see the more
responsible man to take the job.

Well, I can see some
who have some notion of responsibility, and that this government has not. The art of government, to this administration, consists in taking the most circuitous and long-winded route by way of evading every responsibility they confront. That seems to be what they keep themselves in office for.
There was an investigation by commission in the case of the Farmers' Bank, and why? I remember it; it was some years ago, I do
not say I remember it with absolute accuracy. But in that case there was a division of statement as respects certain representations made that were not in writing, as respects certain warnings given to the then minister of finance in relation to the issue of the charter of that bank, and which could only have been made clear and only have been established by something in the nature of a judicial investigation. So far as I can recall, no committee investigation was asked for; I do not think there was any asked for and denied. Here, though, the investigation looks to one object and one alone, an object much narrower than that in the mind of the hon. member, an object that will be defeated if the commission alone is relied on and an object that will be indefinitely postponed if the amendment is adopted. Mr. Speaker, I desire to
occupy the time of the House just for a moment. In view of what the right hon. leader of the opposition, (Mr. Meighen) has said one or two remarks on my part may not be out of place before the debate concludes.
In the first place it is desirable that the House should understand just how the government came to take the course it did in this matter. The matter came to the government's attention officially through a deputation representative of the depositors of the Home Bank. The depositors are the persons most interested in this matter; indeed, the House is debating the subject because the House realizes that a very large number of men and women in this country have lost sums of money and have endured great hardship as a result of the failure of this bank. They feel, and I think rightly feel, that it has been through no fault of theirs that the bank has failed; they wish if possible to have their losses recouped, and they have asked the government whether it would consider the recouping of those losses. It is from the point of view of the depositors and from the desire of the government to consider their wishes and to see that their representations are fully considered by parliament, that we	are discussing the matter at all.
It was the depositors we were considering; that being the case we acted upon the representations made by the depositors themselves.
I was amazed to hear the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) say that the depositors had framed their resolution at the instance of one who was a political friend of the government. His insinuation, if not, indeed, his direct statement, was to the effect that there was some arrangement between the government and the solicitor in virtue of which representations were made in this manner; that, in other words, there were political considerations at the bottom of the representations that were made. I am sorry that the exMinister of Finance is not in his seat; I should like to tell him that his remarks in that connection were unprofessional, were unparliamentary, and 'certainly unworthy of himself. He referred to Mr. Lee who was one of the counsel for the depositors. ]\ 1 r. Lee is a gentleman of high professional standing, a gentleman whose sense of honour is as high as that of any honourable member of this parliament, and I think it ill becomes a* ex-minister of the Crown and a member of parliament, under the privilege of parliament which shields him but which does not permit of any reply to his remarks being made on the floor of the House 
by the person attacked, to direct an insinuation or to make a charge of that character against a member of the legal profession in high standing. I would like to point out that Mr. Lee was not the only gentleman who came before the government representing the depositors in this matter. The deputation which appeared before the government, and which, I may say, was received by all members of the government, came to Ottawa on January 23. Mr. Lee was one of the speakers on that occasion, but other members of the legal profession and members of other professions also spoke and presented the case of the depositors to the government. Mr. R. J. McLauchlin,
K.C., of Toronto, spoke on behalf of the depositors and made representations to the government in this matter. I remarked, Mr. Speaker, that at the time of the presentation of this petition there were several gentlemen who spoke to it, and as I listened to the petition being read it seemed to my mind to carry the implication that the Minister of Finance of that day for some reason or another had not carried out what he should have carried out by way of investigation in accordance with the law existing at the time. The elaboration of their remarks caused me to ask of the deputation at the time, on what ground they were asking the government to indemnify the depositors for their losses. I pointed out to them that they had really presented what seemed to me to be two diametrically opposite points of view. One was that the minister of finance of the day had taken the course that he did for public reasons, that he had not complied with the act in some part for public reasons. Another view was that he had taken the course he did because of some neglect or oversight, that he had shifted his responsibility on to some other person. He had made casual inquiries, and had referred the matter to the late Mr. Lash, I think it was, of Toronto, and that he had not gone into the matter as fully as he should have done so I asked the deputation at the time: On what ground are
Home Bank Investigation

you basing your claim? Is it on the ground of neglect on the part of the Minister of Finance of the day to do his duty, or is it on the ground of his having failed, because of some public reason, to do a certain thing which the law requires? And the answer I received was that in a court of law it was permissible to plead alternatives, and that they were there for the purpose of presenting both points of view. I contend, Mr. Speaker, that using the word "charge" in the sense I meant it, namely, a reflection Qn the Minister of Finance, is the essence of the ground upon which the appeal is being made to the government. The whole ground upon which the depositors have asked the government to see they are indemnified in this matter is that of a certain neglect of duty or failure to perform duty for a public reason or for some other reason, on the part of a previous minister of finance. That is the ground.
Now if this government were to attempt to pass upon that, what would be said? We are being asked to-night not to treat this question in a political, partisan fashion. But were we to say that Sir Thomas White had not done his duty, and to ask this country to pay so many millions of dollars to the depositors because a previous minister of finance had not done his duty while he was in office, what would be said about this administration? From one end of the country to the other it would be heralded abroad that the government had taken advantage of a political opponent, and out of the public treasury had spent this vast sum of money in order to secure political advantage. If in any way this government were to attempt to pass judgment on any of its predecessors in office who were of a different political party, it would be said that our reason for doing so was because we saw in it a political advantage. That is the one thing, Mr. Speaker, we desire the people of this country to know we are not seeking. We wish no political advantage in this matter. We want this question removed from the realm of politics altogether. We want fair play and justice done in this matter in as fair a way as justice can possibly be done.
The question then presented itself, how was an investigation to be made? My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition has spoken about the government having responsibility. He is sometimes fond of asserting that he himself has responsibility, and will carry it out. Hon. gentlemen opposite of the Progressive group, or rather, my hon. friend from East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) representing, I think, in part those who sit 
in the Progressive group, has brought forward a resolution in this House. One of the members of the Liberal party, on this side, has moved an amendment. The government will accept that amendment in full. We will take that responsibility. Now will my right hon. friend and some of his friends show . where they stand by moving an amendment to the amendment? We have made our position clear. All hon. members in the House, with the exception of my right hon. friend, and his supporters, have made their position clear. My right hon. friend is the only leader of a party who is not prepared to stand up and say whether he would or would not settle this matter on some particular line. We have taken a position. We realized that an investigation was necessary, and I contend, Mr. Speaker, that, without investigation, the public ;of this country would never have sanctioned for one minute action on the part of the government in this matter. It is unthinkable that, without any investigation, the government of to-day on the representations of depositors alone, with reference to a matter which took place some years ago, would ask parliament to vote so many millions of dollars out of the public treasury to indemnify depositors for their losses. An investigation is absolutely necessary in this matter. Now an investigation could be of one form or another. We could either have had a parliamentary investigation-could have had this matter referred to a special committee of parliament-or a judicial investigation. Those are the alternatives. Assuming that we had adopted the plan of having a parliamentary investigation, assuming that when parliament met we had said "We have decided to refer this matter to a committee of parliament, to a special committee, my right hon. friend', the leader of the opposition, would hardly have waited to draw a breath until he would have jumped to his feet and declared "The government has a majority on that committee and is doing what it likes in the matter." We realized the tactics of my right hon. friend, we realized the attitude that parliament, would have a perfect right to take towards any action of that kind, we surrounded this matter with the greatest care and caution-

The Prime Minister will permit me to say, in view of the fact that I have already spoken, that he has no right to misrepresent me. I did not say that the government should have referred the matter to investigation by committee. When I spoke I said the government had the facts

When it came to the matter of a judicial inquiry the government was anxious that whoever was chosen should be chosen from another part of the Dominion. I mean from a part of Canada that was not immediately interested in this matter. Many names naturally presented themselves to the government when we were selecting a commissioner. We might have taken a commissioner from Montreal, Toronto, or from Winnipeg or elsewhere. As my hon. friend from East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) mentioned this afternoon, this failure affected people from the province of Quebec out to the Rocky mountains but it did not affect, I think, any persons from the Maritime provinces. It was for that reason the government went to the Maritime provinces and chose as commissioner to investigate this matter, the chief justice of one of the courts, who as commissioner receives no salary for the services he is rendering. The government's whole course was taken with a view of inspiring confidence on the part of the members of this House, on the part of the public, and particularly on the part of the depositors who are most affected.	.
Now, as to the matter of the correspondence, to which my right hon. friend has referred, let me repeat that the communication spoken of that was in the possession of Sir Thomas White and was passed on by him to
Sir Henry Drayton was, so far as the government has any knowledge of it at all, a private document in the possession of these ministers or their private secretaries. Let me direct the attention of the House to this circumstance:	The gentleman who was secretary to Sir Thomas White was also the private secretary to his successor, Sir Henry Drayton, when the latter became Minister of Finance. Sir Thomas White when he left the Finance department gave certain instructions to his secretary, left certain papers with him, told him that some of these papers were to be given to Sir Henry Drayton.

My right hon. friend will recall that when he left office he had a private secretary or a couple of private secretaries; that when he left the position which he formerly held he took with him a large part of the correspondence of the office of Prime Minister, and it was quite right that he should. Some of it he subsequently returned, some of it could not be found anywhere and on this account I asked if I could not obtain it and he had it sent over to me a week or two later iby the private secretary who had it. I want you to give me his private papers, the documents that he has left with you." Had I done that I should have felt that I was taking an extraordinary course, and I should think no person who had been secretary to a minister who would be prepared to hand over documents to his successor without instructions, would be worthy of a position of confidence in the government service.

There is one circumstance, however, I would like to bring to the attention of the House: The administration is convinced of the necessity of having an investigation into this matter. We want the public to know the truth about these papers. Unfortunately the Minister of Finance, through illness, is unable to be in his seat. He told me in his own room, and I talked with him at his bedside, that he had no knowledge whatever that any of these papers were in existence until after he read about them in .the press and discovered that there were some documents which he had not seen and has not seen yet.
